description: We are The_Martians_66 team, a passionate team of Computer Science and AI students interested in game development, 3D graphics, and innovative technologies. We're creating Mars Mission , an immersive Mars exploration game. Our strengths include programming, problem-solving, creativity, and teamwork. We're looking for motivated members skilled in game development, Blender, UI/UX, or programming. Join us to learn, collaborate, and bring exciting ideas to life!
summary:
Our project is an interactive game that allows students to connect space science to hands-on experiencing. The problem with available space resources is that they are isolated from each other, thus students lack the opportunity to experience how these fields actually interact in a space mission. It is composed of leveled missions according to complexity with interactive real-world space exploration scenarios. 
It addresses the challenge by putting students in the role of mission designers. Through complex missions based on real space-exploration scenarios, players get to understand how to organize competing demands and understand their trade offs. A decision made early in the mission can affect what happens later, allowing students to experience the consequences practically.
Our goal is to make learning space science and designing missions understandable through experimentation rather than abstract information. Instead of learning space design through isolated facts about physics, spacecraft, or orbital mechanics, our game brings together these fields in one experience that let's students learn by making descions and understand their consequences directly.
details:
The core concept of our project is a game that serves as a simulator for NASA space missions. It allows players to select, assemble, and construct spacecraft, equipping them with the necessary communication systems and hardware tailored to the requirements of each specific mission. The component selection system is designed so that every part influences other variables, such as mass, energy consumption, and velocity; for instance, increasing the spacecraft's mass requires more energy for launch. The simulation encompasses the entire launch process, including orbital calculations, spacecraft velocity, travel time, and distance, while also simulating ground-based space control centers.

Our project simulates space missions rooted in science fiction narratives, yet grounded in the scientific concepts and data actually used by NASA. This provides users with an immersive experience of a realistic space mission, while simultaneously educating them about space physics and NASA’s latest scientific research. It does so in an entertaining way, encouraging users to learn more about space and experience the challenges faced by real-life astronauts.

Game Mechanics

At the start, the player selects their preferred language (Arabic or English) and chooses the color of their astronaut’s suit, the character they will control. The player then selects one of three available missions. Once a mission is chosen, the player proceeds to build and assemble their spacecraft, outfitting it with the necessary equipment and power systems. Finally, the player embarks on the selected mission.

The first mission is as follows:

Objective:

Design and operate an early-warning spacecraft, named SENTINEL-1. Located at the Sun–Earth L1 Lagrange point, the spacecraft measures solar wind and magnetic fields, providing a warning to Earth before a solar storm arrives. While it offers extra time for protective measures, it cannot prevent the storm itself.

The Story

In 2036, a solar storm, reminiscent of the Carrington Event of 1859, threatens satellites, telecommunication networks, power grids, and the crew of the lunar station, ARGUS. The question is: if such a storm were to strike again, would humanity be prepared?

The Player’s Challenge

Designing the Spacecraft: Selecting instruments, power systems, and communication equipment, all while adhering to strict mass and power constraints.

Launch and Operation: Choosing a launch vehicle, activating the instruments, and ensuring a stable communication link.

Facing the Storm: Classifying solar flares, tracking Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), and monitoring the Bz component and solar wind speed.

Making Tough Decisions: Preparing shelters at the ARGUS station, prioritizing the protection of satellites and power grids, and deciding whether to issue an early warning, risking lower certainty, or wait for further confirmation.

The Outcome: Depending on the player’s design choices, operational execution, and decision-making, the result could range from a well-prepared response to a catastrophic failure of critical infrastructure.

The Impact

Students learn about Lagrange points, solar wind, magnetic fields, the impact of space weather on satellites and power grids, and how to design a mission under specific constraints.

They gain firsthand experience in how initial design decisions ultimately dictate the success or failure of a mission. The importance of early warning systems is made clear through the use of real data from NASA and NOAA, with simulation parameters explicitly highlighted.

The second mission is based on a science fiction narrative: thirty years ago, a space station on Mars was destroyed by the impact of a meteor or comet. In the present day, the player, taking on the role of a character named Nolan, receives a mysterious signal from that very same Martian station. This discovery sparks concern and suspicion at the space center on Earth, prompting Nolan to travel to Mars to investigate the source of the signals.

Throughout this journey, the player engages in simulations of actual launch and landing procedures used in space exploration. By simulating the voyage, the player learns scientific principles, such as the mechanics of launching, landing, and the effects of gravity on various celestial bodies. Additionally, the player must construct an array of solar panels, learning the real-world principles of orienting them toward the Sun to maximize energy generation.

Furthermore, this mission incorporates a recent scientific research initiative from NASA, a sample-return mission targeting Mars’ moons, Phobos and Deimos (part of the "New Frontiers" program, which aims to uncover the origins of these moons by bringing samples back to Earth; see: https://www1.grc.nasa.gov/facilities/compass-lab/designs-by-type/). By weaving these concepts into an entertaining story, the game provides an engaging educational experience.

Fun for the player

Mission 3 consists of:

Objective

Design and operate an early-warning spacecraft, named SENTINEL-1, positioned at the Sun–Earth L1 Lagrange point. Its purpose is to measure solar wind and magnetic fields, providing a warning to Earth before a solar storm arrives. While the spacecraft offers extra time for protective measures, it cannot prevent the storm itself.

The Scenario

In 2036, a solar storm, reminiscent of the 1859 Carrington Event, threatens satellites, telecommunication networks, power grids, and the crew of the lunar station, ARGUS. The question is: if such a storm were to strike again, would humanity be prepared?

The Player’s Challenge

Designing the spacecraft: Selecting instruments, power systems, and communication hardware, all while adhering to strict mass and power constraints.

Launching and operating: Choosing a launch vehicle, activating the onboard instruments, and ensuring a stable communication link.

Facing the storm: Classifying solar flares, tracking Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), and monitoring the Bz component and solar wind speed.

Making difficult decisions: Preparing shelters at the ARGUS station, prioritizing the protection of satellites and infrastructure, and deciding whether to issue an early warning, balancing the need for speed against the risk of lower certainty.

The Outcome: Depending on the player’s performance in design, operations, and decision-making, the result could range from a well-prepared response to the failure of critical infrastructure.

Educational Impact

Students learn about Lagrange points, solar wind, magnetic fields, the impact of space weather on satellites and power grids, and the complexities of mission design under specific constraints. Users can personally experience how initial design decisions ultimately determine the outcome of a mission. They gain an understanding of why early warning systems are critical, using real data from NASA and NOAA, with simulation parameters clearly defined.

A key benefit of our project is that it offers a comprehensive game simulating actual space missions. This allows players to experience life as real astronauts, learning about scientific concepts and space exploration in an entertaining way. By incorporating science fiction narratives into the missions, the project makes scientific content and space-related concepts accessible and engaging, enabling users, including students, to grasp complex ideas through practical application.

Our project aims to support individuals with varying levels of prior knowledge regarding space and the principles of astrophysics. Through science fiction-themed simulations, users can apply scientific information in a hands-on environment, learning about complex concepts and recent discoveries in an enjoyable manner. Furthermore, it helps students bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application, turning the study of scientific concepts into an engaging, hands-on experience.

Our project features a novel element: the simulation tasks are structured around engaging, imaginative, and dramatic narratives that incorporate key scientific concepts. Grounded in authentic scientific data from NASA, the project allows players to enjoy an immersive, fictional story while learning about fundamental scientific principles and NASA’s latest space explorations. Furthermore, it enables students to apply theoretical scientific concepts in a practical, hands-on manner.

Technical Implementation, Tools, and Hardware

We built OUTERRA in Godot 4.3, a free and open-source game engine, using the GL Compatibility renderer so the same project runs on desktop and in the browser. All gameplay, the 3D scenes, the spacecraft, the characters and the user interface are written in GDScript, Godot’s built-in scripting language. Most 3D models are built in code from simple shapes, so no external 3D assets were needed. Mission settings, spacecraft parts and the simulated space-weather scenario are stored in JSON data files, so values can be changed without changing code. The science calculations (power, energy, data, light travel time and solar-wind warning time) are separate scripts. Automated headless tests in Godot play all three missions from start to end, in both English and Arabic.

The game is exported to HTML5/WebAssembly and hosted on GitHub Pages, so it runs free in any modern browser with no installation or account. The Arabic version uses a language system we wrote in GDScript, with right-to-left text and the open-source Baloo Bhaijaan 2 font. Other fonts: Orbitron, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono and DejaVu Sans.

Supporting tools: Python scripts to build the English and Arabic text tables, FFmpeg to edit the demo video, Kokoro TTS (open-source) for the AI-generated voice-over, and Chromium/Playwright to test the web version. We used Claude (an Anthropic AI assistant) to help write code, text and data, under the team’s direction and review.

the creative side

The innovative aspect of our project lies in the fact that the game is more than just a simulation of a space mission; each mission features an engaging, science-fiction-based narrative that is firmly rooted in scientific principles and space exploration. Players become fully immersed in this world as they navigate through missions and their associated challenges. These science-fiction storylines serve as a vehicle for teaching users about concepts in space physics and recent discoveries by NASA. By integrating this scientific information, such as the mechanics of launch, landing, and space travel, directly into the unfolding narrative, the game provides an experience that is both highly entertaining and educational.
